pages.title: TDR
pages.for: A TDR gives the cable's length, its joints, and faults under about 100 Ω, each as a distance from the end you test from. At commissioning, it records the cable's fingerprint.
pages.rule:
L = t × v ÷ 2
v = 2L ÷ t, on a known length
VF = v ÷ 299.8

Up: the impedance rose, as at an open or a break. Down: it fell, a short or low-resistance fault.
Small up then down: a joint.
Far end linked, then open: the reflection that flips is the end.
Red to conductor, black to screen. Dead cable only.
Pulse width: start short. A wider pulse reaches further but hides changes near the set.
XLPE is typically 162 to 186 m/µs. A set that asks for v/2 takes half.
From both ends, the two distances add up to the length.

traps.text: Leaving out the ÷ 2. The time covers the trip there and back.
Leaving a default velocity set. On String B's practice figures, it gives 914.4 m instead of 960.1 m.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A reflection comes back after 20.0 µs. The velocity is set at 160 m/µs. How far away is the reflection?
pages.alt: L = t × v ÷ 2 = 20.0 × 160 ÷ 2 = 1600 m. The time covers the trip there and back, so you halve it. The 3200 m answer leaves out the ÷ 2. The 800 m answer puts in half the velocity and then halves again.
pages.html:
L = t × v ÷ 2 = 20.0 × 160 ÷ 2 = 1600 m.

The time covers the trip there and back, so you halve it. The 3200 m answer leaves out the ÷ 2. The 800 m answer puts in half the velocity and then halves again.

pages.name: What it is for
pages.text:
A TDR sends a short pulse down a core and its screen, and times what comes back. It needs two conductors running side by side. Here they are the core and its own screen. From the echoes it gives the cable's length, where its joints are, and where a low-resistance fault, a break or water is. It draws a map of the cable.

The map recorded at commissioning is the cable's fingerprint. Later traces are compared with it. A joint shows on a trace much like a small fault, so its place must be known in advance.

The TDR goes on a dead cable only. The cable is isolated, discharged and earthed at both ends, as for every test. There is a technician at each end. The pulse is low voltage, a fixed 50 V on some sets.

If it is skipped

Skip it, and all you know is that L2 has a fault somewhere in 2.40 km of cable on the seabed.

pages.name: The why: up and down
pages.text: The pulse sees the cable as an impedance of its own. The cable's inductance and capacitance per metre set it. That is the characteristic impedance, Z0. While Z0 stays the same, the pulse runs on and nothing comes back. Where the impedance changes, part of the pulse reflects. The share that comes back is ρ = (Z load − Z0) ÷ (Z load + Z0). An open end is an infinite impedance, so ρ = +1. The whole pulse comes back the right way up. A short is zero impedance, so ρ = −1. The whole pulse comes back upside down. So a reflection pointing up means the impedance rose. One pointing down means it fell. At a joint the cable's build changes for a short length. The impedance changes and then changes back. So a joint shows as a small up then a small down. A fault from core to screen sits across the line. At the fault the pulse sees two paths in parallel: the fault, and the cable beyond it. Two resistances in parallel give less than either. So the impedance falls, and the reflection points down. For String B, Z0 = 1 ÷ (v × C) = 1 ÷ (168.0 × 10⁶ × 0.22 × 10⁻⁹) = 27.1 Ω. 168.0 m/µs is String B's velocity, found in part (a). 0.22 µF/km is a typical figure. So take 27.1 Ω as a practice value. On a real cable, use the maker's figure. Call the fault's resistance Rf. The load at the fault is Rf in parallel with Z0: Z load = Rf × Z0 ÷ (Rf + Z0). At 35 Ω that is 35 × 27.1 ÷ 62.1 = 15.3 Ω. Put that into the rule, and it becomes ρ = −Z0 ÷ (2 Rf + Z0). The higher Rf, the less it pulls the impedance down. So the dip is smaller. With the far end linked, the end of the cable shows as a downward peak, like a short. Open it, and the end flips to an upward peak. The fault's dip at 11.43 µs points down either way. So the reflection that flips is the end. As the fault resistance rises, the impedance at the fault climbs back towards the cable's 27.1 Ω. So its dip shrinks. It is 0.28 of the pulse at 35 Ω, 0.12 at 100 Ω and 0.01 at 1000 Ω. At 1000 Ω the trace looks like healthy cable. Down then a broad hump: a T joint. Up then a dip: a bridge tap. A sharp up-down spike: a wet splice. A ragged, noisy tail: water getting in. TDR finds faults under about 100 Ω. Above that, a low-voltage pulse will likely not see the fault. Some sets reach about 200 Ω. A high-resistance fault needs other methods. One is arc reflection. A high-voltage surge strikes an arc at the fault. The arc shows on the trace like a short. That is HV work, with its own kit and procedure.
pages.alt: The pulse sees the cable as an impedance of its own. The cable's inductance and capacitance per metre set it. That is the characteristic impedance, Z0. While Z0 stays the same, the pulse runs on and nothing comes back. Where the impedance changes, part of the pulse reflects. The share that comes back is ρ = (Z load − Z0) ÷ (Z load + Z0). An open end is an infinite impedance, so ρ = +1. The whole pulse comes back the right way up. A short is zero impedance, so ρ = −1. The whole pulse comes back upside down. So a reflection pointing up means the impedance rose. One pointing down means it fell.

pages.name: The why: time into distance
pages.text: The TDR measures time. It turns time into distance with the velocity you give it. The pulse goes out and comes back. So the time covers the distance twice: L = t × v ÷ 2. The velocity is often given as a velocity factor, VF = v ÷ c. Here c is the speed of light, 299.8 m/µs. The velocity factor is roughly 1 ÷ the square root of the insulation's relative permittivity. So the insulation sets the velocity, not the copper. Power XLPE typically runs at 0.54 to 0.62, which is 162 to 186 m/µs. Cables differ. So a typical figure is only a starting point. Every distance is its time × v ÷ 2. So a wrong velocity stretches all of them by the same fraction. It never moves one reflection past another. So set the velocity on a length you know. Open the far end, read the end's time, and move the velocity until the end reads the known length. At the default 160 m/µs, the end reads 2285.6 m. That is short of the known 2400 m. The fault reads 914.4 m. The whole trace stretches as the velocity rises. At 168 m/µs the end reads 2399.9 m. That is the known length, to within the rounding of 28.57 µs. The fault then reads 960.1 m. It stays 0.40 of the way along at every setting.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: From the OSS, L2's trace shows a downward peak at 11.43 µs. It stays down when the far end is opened. What is it?
pages.answer: A low-resistance fault from core to screen
pages.alt: String B's figures are practice values. It points down, so the impedance fell there. It did not flip when the far end opened, so it is not the end. The joint at 1620 m would show at 2 × 1620 ÷ 168.0 = 19.29 µs, as a small up then down.
options: A low-resistance fault from core to screen
pages.html:
String B's figures are practice values.

It points down, so the impedance fell there. It did not flip when the far end opened, so it is not the end. The joint at 1620 m would show at 2 × 1620 ÷ 168.0 = 19.29 µs, as a small up then down.

pages.name: Worked example
pages.text: Setting up, and what a 5% velocity error costs. Take a 2 km cable with the velocity set 5% too high. On a 2 km cable, a velocity set 5% high puts the far end 0.05 × 2000 = 100 m out. Every other distance is 5% out too. Setting v on the known length removes the error, using v = 2L ÷ t.
pages.alt: 1 Set up on the dead cable. It is isolated, discharged and earthed at both ends. Lift the earth from the core under test at your end, under control. Red lead to the conductor, black to the screen. 2 First test with the far end linked, conductor to screen or to earth. Then the far end lifts the link, under control. Test again with it open. The reflection that flips is the end. 3 The rule: L = t × v ÷ 2. Each distance goes up in step with v. 4 So a velocity 5% high makes every distance read 5% long. 5 At the far end of a 2 km cable: 0.05 × 2000 = 100 m out.
pages.html:
1

Set up on the dead cable. It is isolated, discharged and earthed at both ends. Lift the earth from the core under test at your end, under control. Red lead to the conductor, black to the screen.

2

First test with the far end linked, conductor to screen or to earth. Then the far end lifts the link, under control. Test again with it open. The reflection that flips is the end.

3

The rule: L = t × v ÷ 2. Each distance goes up in step with v.

4

So a velocity 5% high makes every distance read 5% long.

5

At the far end of a 2 km cable: 0.05 × 2000 = 100 m out.

6

The cure: set v on the known length. With the far end open, v = 2L ÷ t.

7

When you finish, put the earths back on at both ends.

String B: the cable from B01 to the substationScenario

Commissioning tests on a newly laid 66 kV inter-array cable on an offshore wind farm. It runs 2.40 km from turbine B01 to the offshore substation (OSS), the last cable of string B. Three-core, 3 × 240 mm² copper, XLPE, 38/66 (72.5) kV, copper wire screens, armoured, with one field joint 1620 m from the OSS. A technician at each end, talking before every change. The live string A runs in the same corridor. One fault waits to be found. Every figure is a practice value unless it is cited.

Carried forward
(a)String B's VLF test voltage76.0 kV

L2 broke down in the VLF test and now reads 35 Ω from core to screen. Every core is discharged and earthed at both ends. You connect a TDR at the OSS end. On L1, a healthy core, with the far end at B01 open, the end shows at 28.57 µs. The route record gives the length as 2.40 km. These are practice values.

Give it in m/µs, to 1 place.

v = 2L ÷ t

= 2 × 2400 ÷ 28.57 = 168.0 m/µs

VF = 168.0 ÷ 299.8 = 0.56. That is inside the typical 0.54 to 0.62 for XLPE. A set that asks for v/2 takes 168.0 ÷ 2 = 84.0 m/µs.

pages.name: Section A 6(b)
pages.task: Back on L2, test with the far end linked and then open. A downward peak stays at 11.43 µs. (b) Determine the distance to the fault from the OSS.
pages.alt: CARRIED FORWARD (a) Velocity from the open-end reflection 168.0 m/µs Back on L2, test with the far end linked and then open. A downward peak stays at 11.43 µs. Give it in m, to 1 place. L = t × v ÷ 2 = 11.43 × 168.0 ÷ 2 = 960.1 m The joint at 1620 m would show at 19.29 µs. So this is not the joint. Treat 960.1 m as the middle of a search zone. A TDR is generally accurate to within 1% of the cable's length. On String B that is 0.01 × 2400 = 24.0 m either side of 960.1 m.

pages.name: Section A 6(c)
pages.task: (c) Determine the distance to the fault from B01.
pages.why: From B01 = 2400 − 960.1 = 1439.9 m. Now test from B01. The dip should show at 17.14 µs, which is 1439.9 m. Add the distance you measure from B01 to the 960.1 m from the OSS. The two should make 2400 m. If they don't, the velocity is most likely wrong. When the tests are done, put the earths back on at both ends. Record L2: a low-resistance fault from core to screen, 960.1 m from the OSS. The next test, LIRA, checks it from both ends.

pages.name: Section B
pages.task: Explain why the far end is tested linked and then open.
pages.why: A model answer: Linking the far end makes the end of the cable a short. Its reflection points down. Opening it makes the end an open. Its reflection points up. The reflection that flips between the two tests must be the end. A fault along the cable stays the same way up in both. A break also reflects upward. Without the two tests, you could take a break for the end. Once the end is proved, set the velocity so the end reads the cable's known length. Every other distance is then right.

pages.task: Another cable. Its velocity is 172 m/µs, found on a known length. A downward peak shows at 15.00 µs. Determine the distance to it.
